Learning to Remember: End-to-End Training of Memory Agents for Long-Context Reasoning

Kehao Zhang ††thanks: This work was done during Kehao Zhang’s internship at Li Auto Inc. Abstract

Long-context LLMs and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems process information passively, deferring state tracking, contradiction resolution, and evidence aggregation to query time, which becomes brittle under ultra-long streams with frequent updates. We propose the Unified Memory Agent (UMA), an end-to-end reinforcement learning framework that unifies memory operations and question answering within a single policy. UMA maintains a dual memory representation: a compact core summary for global context and a structured Memory Bank that supports explicit CRUD (create, update, delete, reorganize) over key-value entries, enabling proactive consolidation during streaming. To evaluate long-horizon memory behavior, we introduce Ledger-QA, a diagnostic benchmark for continuous state tracking where answers are latent values derived from accumulated updates rather than local span retrieval. Across 13 datasets spanning Ledger-QA, Test-Time Learning, and Accurate Retrieval, UMA substantially outperforms long-context and RAG baselines on dynamic reasoning and learning tasks while remaining competitive on standard retrieval benchmarks, underscoring the importance of learned, end-to-end memory management.

1 Introduction

Context windows of Large Language Models (LLMs) now spanning millions of tokens(Google, 2025; Anthropic, 2025; OpenAI, 2025; Qwen, 2025; Liu et al., 2024), however, long-context models face fundamental challenges beyond window size. First, computational complexity scales quadratically with sequence length in standard attention mechanisms(Vaswani et al., 2017), making processing extremely long contexts prohibitively expensive. Second, empirical studies reveal a context rot phenomenon(Hong et al., 2025): as input length increases, model performance degrades significantly even when all relevant information is present—models struggle to effectively locate and utilize critical details buried within massive contexts.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses scalability by retrieving only relevant passages at query time(Xu et al., 2024), but inherits a deeper limitation shared with long-context approaches: passive information processing. Both paradigms treat context as static raw material, deferring all reasoning to query time. As illustrated in Figure 1, RAG systems must reprocess raw retrieved passages for every query. For reasoning-intensive tasks—such as tracking entity states over time, resolving contradictions, or accumulating evidence from fragmented observations—this causes both accuracy degradation and computational redundancy.

Memory-augmented agents offer a fundamentally different paradigm: proactive reasoning that consolidates information as it arrives rather than reprocessing raw inputs per query. However, existing approaches face critical limitations. Heuristic-based systems like Mem0(Chhikara et al., 2025), Zep(Rasmussen et al., 2025) rely on hand-crafted prompts and memory schemas, lacking task adaptivity. Decoupled architectures such as Memory-R1(Yan et al., 2025) and Mem-alpha(Wang et al., 2025b) separate memory management from task execution through independent training, preventing end-to-end optimization—credit from task outcomes cannot flow back to shape memory decisions.

We propose Unified Memory Agent (UMA), an end-to-end reinforcement learning framework that jointly optimizes memory operations (create, update, delete, reorganize) and task execution within a unified policy. To diagnose proactive reasoning capabilities, we introduce Ledger-QA, a benchmark requiring continuous state tracking where performance directly reflects the ability to consolidate information proactively rather than reprocess raw history per query. We conduct extensive evaluation across 13 datasets spanning three task categories: continuous reasoning (Ledger-QA), test-time learning, and accurate retrieval. Experiments demonstrate that UMA substantially outperforms long-context and RAG baselines on dynamic reasoning tasks while remaining competitive on standard retrieval benchmarks, with ablations confirming the necessity of end-to-end optimization.

2 Method

2.1 Problem Formulation as MDP

We formulate the long-context reasoning task as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). To handle sequences exceeding the context window, we decompose the input into a stream of chunks C={c1,…,cn}C=\{c_{1},\dots,c_{n}\}. The MDP tuple (𝒮,𝒜,𝒫,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},\mathcal{R}) is defined as follows:

State Space (𝒮\mathcal{S}).

At step tt, the state st=(ℳt,xt,ht)s_{t}=(\mathcal{M}_{t},x_{t},h_{t}) consists of:

  • •

    ℳt=(mc​o​r​e,ℬ)\mathcal{M}_{t}=(m^{core},\mathcal{B}): The dual-component memory, comprising a high-level summary (mc​o​r​em^{core}) and a structured key-value bank (ℬ\mathcal{B}).

  • •

    xtx_{t}: The current input focus. To circumvent context window limits, this is dynamically switched between a local text chunk ckc_{k} (during maintenance) and a specific query qq (during QA).

  • •

    hth_{t}: The immediate interaction history, which buffers recent observations and is periodically cleared to manage context length.

Action Space (𝒜\mathcal{A}).

We unify all operations into a single action space, categorized by the phase of interaction. Crucially, read-only tools are available in both phases to ensure the agent can verify beliefs or query the ledger at any time. Detailed specifications for all tools (inputs/outputs) are provided in Appendix A.

  • •

    Memory Operations (𝒜m​e​m\mathcal{A}_{mem}): Used during the chunk processing phase to maintain the state.

    • –

      Add, Update, Delete: CRUD operations to modify the structured bank ℬ\mathcal{B}.

    • –

      Retrieve, List: Read-only operations to check existing keys or values in ℬ\mathcal{B} before modification.

    • –

      UpdateCore: A special terminal action that commits the current progress to mc​o​r​em^{core} and triggers the transition to the next chunk.

  • •

    QA Operations (𝒜q​a\mathcal{A}_{qa}): Used during the query phase to synthesize the answer.

    • –

      BM25(query), Embedding(query): Hybrid retrieval over raw text chunks CC.

    • –

      Retrieve(key), List(): Access to the structured memory bank ℬ\mathcal{B}.

    • –

      Answer(text): The terminal action to generate the final response.

Transition Dynamics (𝒫\mathcal{P}).

The system evolves through a hierarchical process:

  • •

    Inner Loop: Standard tool actions update ℬ\mathcal{B} or append to hth_{t} without advancing the input stream.

  • •

    Outer Loop: The UpdateCore action triggers a state transition where xtx_{t} advances to ck+1c_{k+1} and hth_{t} is reset.

  • •

    Phase Transition: Upon processing cnc_{n}, the system transitions to the QA phase, where xtx_{t} becomes a query qq sampled from the task distribution P⁡(q|C)P(q|C).

This stochastic transition implies that the optimal policy must construct a memory state ℳn\mathcal{M}_{n} robust enough to maximize the expected return over all potential future queries.

2.2 Unified Memory Agent Architecture

Based on the MDP formulation, UMA employs a unified policy πθ​(at|st)\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t}) to generate actions. The architecture is designed to handle the inputs explicitly as follows:

Input Representation.

At any time step tt, the input context provided to the LLM is a concatenation of four segments:

Inputt=[Is​y​s,mtc​o​r​e,xt,ht]\text{Input}_{t}=[I_{sys},m^{core}_{t},x_{t},h_{t}] (1)
  • •

    System Instruction (Is​y​sI_{sys}): Specifies the phase-specific operational guidelines—governing either memory maintenance or question answering—and defines the available toolset (𝒜m​e​m\mathcal{A}_{mem} or 𝒜q​a\mathcal{A}_{qa}).

  • •

    Core Memory (mtc​o​r​em^{core}_{t}): The evolving high-level summary that provides global context.

  • •

    Current Focus (xtx_{t}): The raw text of the current chunk ckc_{k} (in Phase I) or the user query qq (in Phase II).

  • •

    Interaction History (hth_{t}): The trajectory of recent tool calls and their execution results

The framework of Unified Memory Agent contains two phase, as illustrated in Figure 2.

Phase I: Sequential Memory Maintenance.

For each chunk ckc_{k}, the agent initializes ht=∅h_{t}=\emptyset. It iteratively samples actions

at∼πθ(⋅|Is​y​s,mc​o​r​e,ck,ht)a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|I_{sys},m^{core},c_{k},h_{t}) (2)

The environment executes the tool and appends the result to hth_{t}. This loop continues until the agent outputs UpdateCore, which compresses relevant insights into mc​o​r​em^{core} and advances the process to ck+1c_{k+1}.

Phase II: Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented QA.

After processing the final chunk, the input focus xtx_{t} switches to the query qq. The agent utilizes the fully constructed memory ℳn\mathcal{M}_{n} and an empty history hth_{t}. It can invoke hybrid retrieval tools (accessing both the structured bank via Retrieve and raw text via BM25/Embedding) to gather evidence. The process terminates when the agent generates the Answer action.

2.3 Training: Task-Stratified GRPO

We propose a Task-Stratified Group Relative Policy Optimization algorithm. By viewing GRPO as a Monte Carlo (MC) advantage estimator without a value network, we adapt it to handle the hierarchical structure of our task as illustrated in Figure 3.

2.3.1 Nested Trajectory Sampling

To estimate the value of memory actions effectively, we employ a nested sampling strategy during training. For a given context CC:

  1. 1.

    Memory Rollout: We sample NN distinct memory trajectories {τm​e​m1,…,τm​e​mN}\{\tau_{mem}^{1},\dots,\tau_{mem}^{N}\}, resulting in NN different final memory states {ℳn1,…,ℳnN}\{\mathcal{M}_{n}^{1},\dots,\mathcal{M}_{n}^{N}\}.

  2. 2.

    Query Sampling: For each memory state ℳni\mathcal{M}_{n}^{i}, we sample MM different questions {q1,…,qM}\{q_{1},\dots,q_{M}\} from the dataset.

  3. 3.

    QA Rollout: For each pair (ℳni,qj)(\mathcal{M}_{n}^{i},q_{j}), we generate a QA trajectory τq​ai,j\tau_{qa}^{i,j} and compute its final reward Ri,jR_{i,j}.

This process yields a total of N×MN\times M complete trajectories per update step.

2.3.2 Reward Function

The total reward Ri,jR_{i,j} for a trajectory is a weighted sum of immediate and terminal signals:

Ri,j=λt​o​o​l​rt​o​o​l+ro​u​t​c​o​m​e​(aa​n​s,yj)R_{i,j}=\lambda_{tool}r_{tool}+r_{outcome}(a_{ans},y_{j}) (3)

where rt​o​o​l=Nv​a​l​i​d/Nt​o​t​a​lr_{tool}=N_{valid}/N_{total} represents the success rate of tool invocations (rewarding valid API usage while penalizing syntax errors), and ro​u​t​c​o​m​er_{outcome} evaluates the correctness of the final answer against the ground truth yjy_{j}.

2.3.3 Monte Carlo Advantage Estimation

Standard GRPO estimates the advantage AA by normalizing rewards within a group, using the group mean as the baseline. We extend this to our two-stage process:

Advantage for Memory Steps (Am​e​mA_{mem}).

The "return" of a memory trajectory τm​e​mi\tau_{mem}^{i} is the expected utility it provides for future queries. We estimate this by averaging the rewards of all MM questions associated with it. The baseline is the global average across all NN memory trajectories.

Gim​e​m=1M​∑j=1MRi,j,G¯m​e​m=1N​∑i=1NGim​e​mG_{i}^{mem}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}R_{i,j},\quad\bar{G}^{mem}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}G_{i}^{mem} (4)
Am​e​mi=Gim​e​m−G¯m​e​mσ⁡(Gm​e​m)A_{mem}^{i}=\frac{G_{i}^{mem}-\bar{G}^{mem}}{\sigma(G^{mem})} (5)

This encourages the policy to generate memory states that are robust across diverse queries.

Advantage for QA Steps (Aq​aA_{qa}).

For a specific question qjq_{j}, the difficulty is intrinsic. Therefore, we normalize the reward of a QA trajectory τq​ai,j\tau_{qa}^{i,j} relative only to other trajectories answering the same question qjq_{j} (but based on different memories).

R¯⋅,j=1N​∑k=1NRk,j,Aq​ai,j=Ri,j−R¯⋅,jσ⁡(R⋅,j)\bar{R}_{\cdot,j}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}R_{k,j},A_{qa}^{i,j}=\frac{R_{i,j}-\bar{R}_{\cdot,j}}{\sigma(R_{\cdot,j})} (6)

This isolates the reasoning capability from the question difficulty, ensuring fair credit assignment.

Finally, the policy πθ\pi_{\theta} is updated by maximizing the GRPO objective using these stratified advantages:

𝒥⁡(θ)=1N​M​∑i=1N∑j=1M[ℒm​e​mi+ℒq​ai,j]\begin{split}\mathcal{J}(\theta)=\frac{1}{NM}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\Big[\mathcal{L}_{mem}^{i}+\mathcal{L}_{qa}^{i,j}\Big]\end{split} (7)

where

ℒm​e​mi=∑t∈τm​e​mi[min(ρtAm​e​mi,OPENclip​(ρt,1−ϵ,1+ϵ)​Am​e​mi)−βDK​L(πθ||πr​e​f)t]\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{mem}^{i}=\sum_{t\in\tau_{mem}^{i}}\Big[&\min(\rho_{t}A_{mem}^{i},\\ &\text{clip}(\rho_{t},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)A_{mem}^{i})\\ &-\beta D_{KL}(\pi_{\theta}||\pi_{ref})_{t}\Big]\end{split} (8)
ℒq​ai,j=∑t∈τq​ai,j[min(ρtAq​ai,j,OPENclip​(ρt,1−ϵ,1+ϵ)​Aq​ai,j)−βDK​L(πθ||πr​e​f)t]\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{qa}^{i,j}=\sum_{t\in\tau_{qa}^{i,j}}\Big[&\min(\rho_{t}A_{qa}^{i,j},\\ &\text{clip}(\rho_{t},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)A_{qa}^{i,j})\\ &-\beta D_{KL}(\pi_{\theta}||\pi_{ref})_{t}\Big]\end{split} (9)

Here, ρt=πθ​(at|st)πr​e​f​(at|st)\rho_{t}=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})}{\pi_{ref}(a_{t}|s_{t})} denotes the importance sampling ratio between the current policy πθ\pi_{\theta} and the behavior policy πr​e​f\pi_{ref} used for trajectory collection.

3 The Ledger-QA Benchmark

Existing long-context benchmarks primarily focus on retrieval-centric tasks, where the answer is explicitly located within a specific text span. However, real-world agents often operate in dynamic environments requiring state tracking—continuously updating a structured belief state based on unstructured interactions. To rigorously evaluate this capability, we introduce Ledger-QA, a synthetic benchmark simulating long-horizon personal finance management. Unlike existing datasets derived from static corpora, Ledger-QA is programmatically generated to simulate dynamic state updates over long horizons.

3.1 Dataset Construction

The construction pipeline consists of three stages, designed to mimic the complexity of real-world bookkeeping:

Long-Horizon Timeline Simulation.

We simulate a user’s consumption behavior over a continuous timeline (e.g., a full year). Unlike independent QA samples, the data in Ledger-QA is organized as a chronological stream of NN sessions. Each session corresponds to a specific date, ensuring temporal dependencies.

Natural Dialogue Synthesis.

For each session, we employ an advanced LLM (e.g., Gemini-3-Pro) to synthesize natural user-assistant conversations. To ensure realism and complexity, the generation covers a diverse taxonomy of 8 major consumption categories (e.g., Dining, Transportation) and incorporates significant noise, such as chit-chat, clarifications, and informal expressions. This design forces the agent to filter irrelevant information and precisely extract structured transaction records (Date, Scene, Amount) from the noisy unstructured text.

Ground Truth & Query Generation.

Parallel to the dialogue, we maintain a structured list of ‘Transaction‘ objects to calculate the ground truth. We generate questions that require reasoning over this structured data rather than simple text matching. We design 8 different question categories.

The construction methodology and examples are detailed in Appendix B.

3.2 Why Ledger-QA is Challenging

Ledger-QA fundamentally differs from standard RAG benchmarks by demanding long-horizon state aggregation rather than local information retrieval. Answers (e.g., "Total spending") are latent values derived from summing scattered transactions (v1+⋯+vnv_{1}+\dots+v_{n}) across the entire timeline. This requires the agent to maintain a continuous, high-fidelity belief state, where a single extraction error at any point propagates to the final result, rendering simple retrieval or approximate summarization ineffective.

4 Experiment

4.1 Experimental Setup

4.1.1 Evaluation Benchmarks

To rigorously evaluate the Unified Memory Agent across the full spectrum of memory capabilities—from dynamic updates to static retrieval—we conduct experiments on three distinct categories of tasks.

Dynamic State Tracking.

Existing benchmarks largely focus on read-only retrieval. To evaluate the capability of maintaining and updating a persistent state over long horizons, we utilize our proposed Ledger-QA (described in Section 3). This dataset serves as a litmus test for the agent’s ability to perform precise CRUD operations and maintain a consistent ledger (e.g., calculating running totals) among a stream of noisy dialogue, a capability absent in standard RAG benchmarks.

Test-Time Learning (TTL).

Following the protocol in MemoryAgentBench (Hu et al., 2025), we evaluate on six datasets: TREC-Coarse, TREC-Fine, NLU, Clinic, Banking77, and PubMed-RCT. In these tasks, the input stream consists of labeled examples rather than narrative text. The agent must "learn" classification rules in-context by storing them in memory and subsequently applying this learned knowledge to answer test queries, assessing the agent’s capacity for inductive reasoning via memory construction.

Accurate Retrieval (AR).

To verify that our memory compression and indexing mechanisms preserve fine-grained details, we select seven established benchmarks: HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018), LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024), LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2025), MSC (Xu et al., 2022), PearlTQA (Du et al., 2024), SQuAD (Rajpurkar et al., 2016), and ConvoMem (Pakhomov et al., 2025). These tasks demand high-precision information extraction from long documents or conversation histories.

Evaluation Metric.

Given the open-ended nature of agentic interactions, we employ an LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm for robust evaluation. Specifically, we utilize Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 as the evaluator to assess the correctness of the agent’s answers against the ground truth. The detailed evaluation prompts and scoring criteria are provided in Appendix C.

Detailed statistics and specific taxonomies for all evaluation datasets are provided in Appendix D.

4.1.2 Baselines

We compare UMA against a diverse set of baselines. First, we evaluate standard approaches: Concat, which inputs the full context to test the backbone’s native capacity, and RAG, which retrieves the top-20 chunks using a hybrid strategy combining dense embeddings and sparse BM25 via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). Second, we include recurrent summarization models: MemAgent (Yu et al., 2025) iteratively updates a running memory state based on the query, while MemAgent-woq performs query-agnostic compression, challenging the agent to identify salient information without guidance. Finally, we compare against advanced agentic frameworks: Mem1 (Zhou et al., 2025) interleaves chunk reading with dynamic retrieval to maintain an evolving internal state, and MemAlpha (Wang et al., 2025b) utilizes an RL-optimized policy to manage a composite memory system (core, episodic, and semantic), representing the current state-of-the-art in trainable memory agents. Implementation details are provided in Appendix E.

4.1.3 Implementation Details

Training Dataset Preparation.

To foster a robust policy capable of handling diverse memory operations, we construct a composite training dataset from three sources: (1) Multi-Hop Retrieval Data derived from HotpotQA (Yu et al., 2025) to simulate retrieval-intensive environments; (2) General Long-Context Data adapted from MemAlpha (Wang et al., 2025b); and (3) State-Tracking Data from our synthetic Ledger-QA to target dynamic updates. Detailed statistics for these datasets are provided in Appendix F.

Training Setup.

We implement our framework using a customized version of veRL (Sheng et al., 2024). The policy is initialized from Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct and optimized via Task-Stratified Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on a cluster of 32 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Comprehensive hyperparameters and configuration details are deferred to Appendix G.

4.2 Main Results

Table 1 presents the comparative performance across 13 standard benchmarks. We observe that:

Superiority in Test-Time Learning (TTL).

Our Unified Memory Agent demonstrates exceptional performance on TTL tasks (e.g., Banking77, Clinic, TREC-Fine), consistently surpassing MemAlpha by a large margin. Notably, Banking77 and Clinic were not seen during training, yet our agent achieves 87.00% and 91.00% accuracy respectively, demonstrating that our agent has generalization capabilities.

Robustness in Retrieval & Reasoning.

On Accurate Retrieval (AR) tasks, our method remains highly competitive, highlighting our agent’s capability in handling multi-session dialogues.

4.3 Results on Ledger-QA

To evaluate the capability of dynamic state tracking over long horizons, we test all baselines on the Ledger-QA benchmark with varying session counts N∈{2,5,…,50}N\in\{2,5,\dots,50\}. As shown in Figure 4, the results reveal a distinct separation in performance trends as the timeline extends.

Vulnerability of Baselines.

In short-horizon settings (N≤5N\leq 5), standard approaches like RAG and MemAgent-woq achieve competitive accuracy (70–90%), indicating that static retrieval or simple summarization suffices for limited contexts. However, performance collapses as NN increases. RAG consistently plummets to below 20% at N=50N=50, failing to aggregate scattered updates. Similarly, despite moderate mid-range performance, MemAgent eventually succumbs to context rot and error accumulation, dropping to ∼\sim20%. This confirms that without a persistent structured store, neither retrieval nor implicit compression can sustain long-horizon consistency.

Robustness of Unified Memory Agent.

In contrast, our UMA (pink line) demonstrates exceptional resilience. It consistently outperforms all baselines by a significant margin, particularly in the long-horizon regime (N≥20N\geq 20). Even at the most challenging setting of 50 sessions, UMA maintains an accuracy of over 50%, whereas the best baseline struggles to reach 25%. This validates that our explicit memory operations effectively decouple state maintenance from sequence length, enabling robust bookkeeping even in ultra-long contexts.

4.4 Ablation Studies

To disentangle the contributions of our unified architecture and the reinforcement learning paradigm, we conduct a comprehensive ablation analysis as shown in the bottom section of Table 1.

Impact of Memory Maintenance (Phase I).

We first examine the necessity of the sequential memory maintenance phase by comparing the full architecture against the retrieval-only variants.

  • •

    Without RL: Even using the base model, the agent equipped with memory capabilities (w/o RL, 61.38%) significantly outperforms the stateless baseline (w/o RL & Phase I, 45.26%). This suggests that simply providing the agent with a "write" capability allows for better information retention than reactive retrieval alone.

  • •

    With RL: The gap persists after training. The full UMA achieves 76.46% average accuracy, surpassing the trained retrieval-only agent (w/o Phase I) at 63.81%.

Impact of RL Training.

Next, we evaluate the effectiveness of our Task-Stratified GRPO by comparing the base models with their RL-trained counterparts.

  • •

    On Retrieval-Only Agent: RL training boosts the performance of the retrieval-only agent from 45.26% (w/o RL & Phase I) to 63.81% (w/o Phase I). This demonstrates that our reward mechanism effectively teaches the model to utilize retrieval tools more precisely, even without a persistent memory.

  • •

    On Unified Agent: The gain is equally substantial for the full architecture, rising from 61.38% (w/o RL) to 76.46% (UMA). The base model often struggles to manage the memory lifecycle coherently, whereas the RL-trained policy learns to perform timely updates and precise lookups, unlocking the full potential of the memory bank.

Impact of Stratified Advantage Grouping.

We further validate our Task-Stratified GRPO by comparing it with a Global Group variant that normalizes advantages across all steps indiscriminately. As shown in Table 1, the Global Group variant underperforms our method (73.58% vs. 76.46%). This confirms that mixing heterogeneous rewards (binary QA scores vs. aggregated memory utility) dilutes the learning signal. Our stratified approach, by normalizing within task-specific groups, ensures fairer credit assignment and more effective policy optimization.

Two-Stage vs. Unified End-to-End Training.

We further investigate whether UMA can be learned via a decoupled two-stage pipeline that trains memory maintenance and QA separately (UMA (2 Stage)). As shown in Table 1, this variant reaches 66.29% average accuracy, which is consistently below the jointly-optimized UMA (76.46%). We attribute the gap to a train–test mismatch: optimizing Phase I in isolation cannot anticipate what information will be maximally useful under the final QA policy, while optimizing Phase II cannot retroactively shape upstream memory decisions. In contrast, unified end-to-end RL enables direct credit assignment from QA outcomes back to memory operations, encouraging memory entries that are compact, precise, and future-query-aware.

5 Related Work

Internal Memory and Context Compression. Several approaches extend context by modifying model internals, such as embedding information in parameters (Wang et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025), compressing KV caches (Qian et al., 2025; Li et al., 2024), or utilizing soft prompts (Burtsev et al., 2020; Ge et al., 2023). While offering high inference efficiency, these methods require white-box access and suffer from inherent capacity bottlenecks compared to external architectures (Wang and Chen, 2025), limiting their utility for ultra-long horizons.

Prompt-based External Memory. To bypass internal limits, frameworks like MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) and SCM (Wang et al., 2023) manage external storage via OS-like hierarchies or graph schemas. While compatible with black-box models, they rely heavily on zero-shot instruction following. This creates a dependency on large proprietary models, as smaller models struggle to reliably execute complex memory updates via prompting alone (Wang et al., 2025b), often leading to suboptimal retrieval in dynamic settings.

Trainable Memory Agents. Recent work shifts towards training models for autonomous memory management. Approaches include recurrent compression via RL (Yu et al., 2025), interleaving retrieval with reasoning (Zhou et al., 2025), and utilizing composite memory structures (Yan et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b). Unlike our unified approach, these methods typically decouple memory maintenance from reasoning or rely on transient summaries. Our work advances this domain by unifying memory operations and reasoning into a single policy, enabling more effective cross-session state tracking.

6 Conclusion

In this paper, we proposed the Unified Memory Agent, an end-to-end framework that jointly optimizes memory acquisition and utilization via reinforcement learning. By employing a Task-Stratified GRPO strategy, our method effectively aligns the heterogeneous objectives of long-horizon memory maintenance and downstream question answering. To address the lack of benchmarks for dynamic state tracking, we introduced Ledger-QA, a dataset requiring persistent updates to an evolving ledger. Experimental results demonstrate that our agent significantly outperforms baselines on state-tracking tasks while remaining competitive on standard retrieval benchmarks. Ablation studies confirm the necessity of both the learned policy and the explicit memory update mechanism. Looking forward, our work suggests that robust long-context intelligence demands active, learned state management rather than passive retrieval alone.

Limitations

While our Unified Memory Agent demonstrates promising capabilities, several limitations remain. First, our current implementation enforces a hard context window limit (e.g., 16k tokens) via truncation. Although the memory bank mitigates information loss, an infinite-horizon setting where the agent must manage memory over millions of tokens without any raw context fallback remains an open challenge. Second, the Ledger-QA benchmark, while rigorous, is synthetically generated. Real-world bookkeeping or state-tracking scenarios may involve more unstructured noise and ambiguity than our current simulation covers. Finally, our training relies on a specific set of tools (CRUD + Retrieval); extending this framework to support multi-modal memory (e.g., images, audio) or more complex tool-use patterns requires further investigation.

Appendix A Tool Definitions

Our agent interacts with the environment and its internal state via a structured API. Below we provide the detailed specifications for each tool available in the Memory Toolset (𝒯m​e​m\mathcal{T}_{mem}) and the Retrieval Toolset (𝒯q​a\mathcal{T}_{qa}).

A.1 Memory Toolset (𝒯m​e​m\mathcal{T}_{mem})

Used during the Sequential Memory Maintenance phase to manage the persistent Memory Bank (ℬ\mathcal{B}).

  • •

    Add(key: str, value: str) →\rightarrow str: Creates a new entry in the memory bank. Input: A unique title (key) and the content (value). Output: Returns "Success" if the key is new; returns an error message if the key already exists.

  • •

    Update(key: str, value: str) →\rightarrow str: Modifies an existing entry. Input: The target key and the new value. Output: Returns "Success" if the update is applied; returns an error if the key is not found.

  • •

    Delete(key: str) →\rightarrow str: Removes an entry. Input: The target key. Output: Returns "Success" upon deletion; returns an error if the key does not exist.

  • •

    Retrieve(key: str) →\rightarrow str: Reads the full content of a specific memory. Input: The target key. Output: Returns the stored value string; returns an error if the key does not exist.

  • •

    List() →\rightarrow List[str]: Scans the memory bank. Input: None. Output: Returns a list of all current keys (titles), enabling the agent to survey stored topics before performing operations.

A.2 Retrieval Toolset (𝒯q​a\mathcal{T}_{qa})

Used during the Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented QA phase to fetch information from both the structured memory and the raw context. Note that Retrieve and List are also available in this phase to access the Memory Bank.

  • •

    Embedding(query: str, top_k: int) →\rightarrow List[str]: Performs dense retrieval over the raw context chunks. Input: A search query and the number of chunks to retrieve (top_k). Mechanism: Encodes the query using sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and retrieves the top-kk chunks based on cosine similarity. Output: A list of the most semantically relevant text chunks.

  • •

    BM25(query: str, top_k: int) →\rightarrow List[str]: Performs sparse retrieval over the raw context chunks. Input: A search query and the number of chunks to retrieve (top_k). Mechanism: Uses the BM25 algorithm to match keywords. Output: A list of the top-kk chunks with the highest keyword overlap.

Appendix B Details of Ledger-QA Construction

The construction of the Ledger-QA benchmark employs a three-stage pipeline designed to simulate realistic, long-horizon bookkeeping scenarios. Unlike traditional methods that generate structured data first and then condition the dialogue on it, we employ a joint synthesis strategy. We provide the LLM with high-level user intents (e.g., "wants to buy coffee"), and the LLM simultaneously generates both the natural dialogue and the corresponding structured transaction records. This ensures that details such as amounts and descriptions are contextually appropriate and naturally woven into the conversation.

B.1 Consumption Scene Taxonomy

To simulate a diverse personal finance environment, we define a hierarchical taxonomy of consumption scenes. The dataset covers 8 major categories, each with multiple sub-scenes:

  • •

    Dining: Fast Food, Restaurant, Coffee, Bubble Tea, BBQ, Hot Pot, Snacks, Takeout.

  • •

    Transportation: Subway, Bus, Taxi, Gas, Parking, Train, Flight.

  • •

    Shopping: Clothing, Electronics, Daily Necessities, Cosmetics, Books, Groceries, Furniture.

  • •

    Entertainment: Movie, KTV, Gaming, Gym, Travel, Concert, Escape Room.

  • •

    Utilities: Water & Electricity, Property Fee, Phone Bill, Internet, Gas Bill, Rent.

  • •

    Medical: Medicine, Doctor Visit, Health Checkup, Dental, Glasses.

  • •

    Education: Training Course, Books & Materials, Online Course, Exam Registration, Tuition.

  • •

    Other: Transfer, Red Envelope, Donation, Pet, Beauty & Salon.

B.2 Data Generation Pipeline

Stage 1: Timeline & Scenario Sampling.

For each sample, we first generate a chronological timeline spanning a full year. We randomly sample NN dates (sessions) from this range. For each session, we stochastically select a subset of consumption scenes (e.g., Dining-Coffee, Transportation-Taxi) to form the user’s "intent" for that day.

Stage 2: Joint Dialogue & Transaction Synthesis.

We feed the selected date and scene intents into an advanced LLM (e.g., Gemini-3-Pro). The model is instructed to act as a user-assistant pair and generate a JSON object containing two aligned fields:

  1. 1.

    Dialogue: The natural conversation turns.

  2. 2.

    Transactions: The structured ground truth (Amount, Description, etc.) corresponding to the dialogue.

Crucially, we do not pre-determine the amounts. The LLM decides reasonable amounts based on the context (e.g., $5 for coffee vs. $500 for a flight), ensuring semantic consistency.

Stage 3: Question Generation.

We extract the ground-truth transaction ledger generated in Stage 2 and programmatically generate questions across 8 distinct templates.

The question types include:

  1. 1.

    Time-Range Scene Amount: "How much was spent on Dining from Jan to Mar?"

  2. 2.

    Time-Range Multi-Scene: "Total spending on Dining and Travel in Q1?"

  3. 3.

    Global Total: "What was the total spending across all records?"

  4. 4.

    Max Scene: "Which category had the highest spending?"

  5. 5.

    Max Frequency Date: "On which date were there the most transactions?"

  6. 6.

    Max Single Amount: "What was the largest single transaction?"

  7. 7.

    Point Query: "How much was spent on Coffee on 2024-05-01?"

  8. 8.

    Single Date Scene Amount: "How much was spent on Dining on 2024-05-01?"

B.3 Dataset Statistics

To evaluate the agent’s robustness across varying temporal horizons, we constructed a comprehensive suite of datasets ranging from short-term interactions (2 sessions) to long-horizon histories (50 sessions).

Training Set.

We utilize the 10-session configuration for training, consisting of 200 samples with over 6,000 questions. This provides a balanced difficulty level for the agent to learn state-tracking policies.

Test Set.

The test set is stratified by session count (N∈{2,5,10,20,30,40,50}N\in\{2,5,10,20,30,40,50\}). Detailed statistics for each configuration are presented in Table 3.

B.4 Generation Algorithm

The core logic of our joint synthesis pipeline is formalized in Algorithm 1.

Appendix C Evaluation Prompts

To ensure consistent and fair evaluation, we employ an LLM-as-a-Judge approach using Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507. The specific prompts used for different benchmarks are detailed below.

General Prompt.

For all benchmarks except LongMemEval, we utilize a unified evaluation template designed to assess semantic correctness:

"I will give you a question, a correct answer, and a response from a model. Please answer yes if the response contains the correct answer. Otherwise, answer no. If the response is equivalent to the correct answer or contains all the intermediate steps to get the correct answer, you should also answer yes. If the response only contains a subset of the information required by the answer, answer no.

Question: {question}

Correct Answer: {answer}

Model Response: {prediction}

Is the model response correct? Answer yes or no only."

LongMemEval Prompts.

Following the official implementation (Wu et al., 2025), we apply task-specific prompts to handle the nuances of different reasoning types (e.g., temporal reasoning, knowledge updates).

  • •

    Default / Fact Retrieval: Same as the General Prompt above.

  • •

    Temporal Reasoning: Adds tolerance for off-by-one errors:

    "…In addition, do not penalize off-by-one errors for the number of days. If the question asks for the number of days/weeks/months, etc., and the model makes off-by-one errors (e.g., predicting 19 days when the answer is 18), the model’s response is still correct…"

  • •

    Knowledge Update: Allows inclusion of previous information if the update is correct:

    "…If the response contains some previous information along with an updated answer, the response should be considered as correct as long as the updated answer is the required answer…"

  • •

    Single-Session Preference: Evaluates personalization based on a rubric:

    "…Please answer yes if the response satisfies the desired response… The response is correct as long as it recalls and utilizes the user’s personal information correctly.

    Rubric: {rubric}…"

  • •

    Abstention: Checks for correct identification of unanswerable questions:

    "…Please answer yes if the model correctly identifies the question as unanswerable. The model could say that the information is incomplete…

    Explanation: {explanation}

    Does the model correctly identify the question as unanswerable? Answer yes or no only."

Appendix D Evaluation Dataset Details

We employ a diverse set of benchmarks to evaluate the agent’s capabilities. Detailed statistics for all evaluation datasets are summarized in Table 3. Below we detail the preprocessing and construction logic for each dataset, corresponding to the implementation in our codebase.

D.1 Dynamic State Tracking

Ledger-QA (Synthetic).

As detailed in Appendix B, we generate synthetic bookkeeping data. In our experiments, we utilize the configuration of 10 sessions per sample to balance complexity and evaluation speed.

D.2 Test-Time Learning (TTL)

For TTL tasks, we source data from MemoryAgentBench (Hu et al., 2025). To ensure the agent understands the classification nature of these tasks, we prepend a specific instruction hint to each query if not already present:

"Sentence: {original_query}
What are the labels for the above sentence?"

D.3 Accurate Retrieval (AR)

HotpotQA.

Following MemAgent (Yu et al., 2025), we ensure strict data isolation by using non-overlapping training and validation splits. We inject ground-truth documents into 200 shuffled distractors, requiring the agent to retrieve evidence from the chunked stream to solve multi-hop queries without any risk of data leakage.

LoCoMo.

We adapt prompts for specific question categories to ensure valid evaluation:

  • •

    Temporal (Cat 2): We append "Use DATE of CONVERSATION to answer with an approximate date" to guide relative time reasoning.

  • •

    Adversarial (Cat 5): We convert these into a multiple-choice format "(A) {distractor} (B) Not mentioned" (with randomized order). The agent must select "Not mentioned" to demonstrate correct rejection of unanswerable queries.

LongMemEval.

We utilize the longmemeval_s subset. Questions are timestamped (e.g., [2024-01-01] Question...) to provide temporal context.

MSC (Multi-Session Chat).

We use a modified version of MSC introduced by MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) provided at https://huggingface.co/datasets/MemGPT/MSC-Self-Instruct. To increase context length, we batch 5 base samples into a single evaluation instance (batch_size=5). Each instance thus contains 25 sessions (5 samples ×\times 5 sessions), and the agent is queried about specific details from any of the batched conversations.

ConvoMem.

We filter the pre_mixed_test-
cases provided at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Salesforce/ConvoMem/tree/main to select only those with a total conversation length exceeding 2 million characters to ensure they qualify as long-context tasks. Each conversation turn is formatted as "{Speaker}: {Text}". We choose the user_evidence category for evaluation.

Appendix E Baseline Implementation Details

We implement the baseline methods Mem1 and MemAlpha using the codebase provided at https://github.com/wangyu-ustc/Mem-alpha. For all experiments, we enforce a strict context window limit of 16k tokens. When the total input length (including memory/context, query, and instructions) exceeds this limit, we apply left-truncation to the memory or context sequence, retaining only the most recent tokens to fit within the 16k window.

Backbone Models.

To isolate the contribution of the memory mechanism, we standardize the backbone model where possible:

  • •

    Standard Backbone: Unless otherwise specified (e.g., for Concat, RAG, MemAgent), we utilize Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 for both the context processing and final QA phases.

  • •

    Specialized Memory Models: For baselines that require specific pre-trained weights for memory operations, we follow their original configurations:

    • –

      Mem1: Uses Mem-Lab/Qwen2.5-7B-RL-
      RAG-Q2-EM-Release       for the memory formation phase.

    • –

      MemAlpha: Uses YuWangX/Memalpha-4B for the memory formation phase.

    Crucially, for the final Question Answering phase, both Mem1 and MemAlpha revert to the standard Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 backbone to ensure a fair comparison of reasoning capabilities.

Appendix F Training Data Details

Table 4 summarizes the detailed statistics of the datasets utilized in our training phase.

Data Sources.

Our training data is curated from three main sources: (1) HotpotQA (Modified): We construct a retrieval-intensive version of HotpotQA following the protocol in MemAgent (Yu et al., 2025), augmenting each sample with 200 documents. (2) Ledger-QA (Synthetic): We generate a specialized dataset for dynamic state tracking as described in Section 3. (3) MemAlpha Corpus: For all other datasets (SQuAD, PerLTQA, NLU, TREC, PubMed, BookSum), we directly incorporate the high-quality training corpus provided by MemAlpha (Wang et al., 2025b) to ensure broad coverage of reasoning tasks (provided at https://huggingface.co/datasets/YuWangX/Memalpha-full).

Data Isolation.

We strictly enforce data isolation to prevent leakage. For HotpotQA, we follow the MemAgent protocol, constructing our training and evaluation sets from the original HotpotQA training and validation splits, respectively. For Ledger-QA, the training and test samples are synthesized independently with distinct seed parameters. For the MemAlpha Corpus, we utilize the official training split provided by the authors, ensuring zero overlap with the evaluation benchmarks used in our experiments.

Consistent with our dual-track training strategy (see Appendix G), the Generalist Agent is trained on the combination of HotpotQA and MemAlpha corpus to foster broad generalization, while the Specialist Agent is fine-tuned specifically on the Ledger-QA dataset. To maintain training efficiency, for MemAlpha corpus containing a large number of queries per instance (e.g., SQuAD, NLU), we randomly sample up to 10 queries per training sample.

Appendix G Training Configuration

We implement our training framework based on a customized version of veRL (Sheng et al., 2024), optimized for multi-conversation and multi-turn agent rollouts. The policy model is initialized from Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct and optimized using AdamW with a learning rate of 1×10−61\times 10^{-6}. We employ the Task-Stratified Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm with a group size of G=16G=16 samples per context and a KL divergence penalty coefficient of β=0.001\beta=0.001.

To balance generalization across diverse tasks with the specific demands of intensive state tracking, we adopt a dual-track training strategy:

  • •

    Generalist Agent (for TTL & AR): To ensure robust performance across broad retrieval and reasoning tasks, this model is trained on the combined Multi-Hop and General Long-Context datasets for 2 epochs.

  • •

    Specialist Agent (for Ledger-QA): Given the unique requirement for continuous numerical updates and long-horizon consistency in Ledger-QA, we train a separate model specifically on the Ledger-QA training set. This model is trained for 6 epochs to fully adapt to the state-tracking dynamics, allowing us to probe the architectural upper bound for this specialized domain.

All experiments are conducted on a cluster of 32 NVIDIA H200 GPUs (4 nodes ×\times 8 GPUs). To manage memory efficiency during long-horizon rollouts, we utilize vLLM for inference with a tensor parallelism size of 1 and set the GPU memory utilization to 0.5. The maximum sequence length for both prompts and responses is set to 8,192 tokens. The total training time spans approximately 2 days for the Generalist Agent and 0.5 days for the Specialist Agent.

Appendix H Detailed Evaluation Metrics

In addition to the accuracy metric reported in the main text, we provide the Exact Match (EM), F1, and ROUGE scores for all evaluated benchmarks to offer a more granular view of model performance. Table 5 presents the Exact Match scores, which measure the percentage of predictions that match the ground truth verbatim. Table 6 presents the F1 scores, which account for partial overlaps between the prediction and the reference answer. Table 7 presents the ROUGE-L scores, evaluating the lexical overlap and fluency of the generated responses.
